note: The Investor desk syllabus. Levels unlock in order; each lesson is played card-by-card, not read as a wall of text. Education only — CLAUDE.md Rule 5: this teaches how to read the market, never what to buy. `anatomy` cards render an interactive labelled document; where the desk holds a real reported figure it is shown and sourced, and where it does not the line is marked as something to find in the actual filing. No company number is ever invented.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.blurb: What you are actually buying, where it trades, what it costs you, and the money rules that decide whether any of this goes well.

lessons.title: What a share actually is
lessons.why: Most people meet the market as rumours and tips. It is simpler, and much less exciting, than that.

cards.h: You are buying a piece of a business
p: A share is a slice of ownership in a real company. Buy one share of a cement maker and you own a genuine — very small — piece of its factories, its cash, its debts, and every rupee of profit it earns from here on.
That is the whole idea. Everything else in this course is a tool for judging that slice.

cards.h: Nobody sets the price for you
p: The number on the screen moves because other people are changing their minds about what that slice is worth. The exchange does not decide it. Your broker does not decide it.
It is simply where buyers and sellers currently agree.

cards.h: Two things that make shares different
p: A share can lose value permanently if the business gets worse. There is no floor under it.
And it has no maturity date. Nobody owes you your money back on a fixed day, the way a bank deposit or a National Savings certificate does.
The question is never 'will this go up?' It is 'is this a business I understand, at a price that makes sense?'

lessons.takeaway: You are buying a piece of a business, not a ticket in a draw.

check.q: You buy shares and the price falls 30% the next month. What has actually happened?
options: The exchange lowered the price
Buyers and sellers now value the business lower than you paid
You owe the company money
check.explain: Price is just where the market currently agrees. It tells you what people think today — not whether the business itself got worse. Working out which of the two happened is the real skill.

lessons.title: The PSX, and what KSE-100 really measures
lessons.why: You will hear 'the market was up today' constantly. Worth knowing exactly what that sentence measures.

cards.h: The exchange is a venue, not a seller
p: The Pakistan Stock Exchange is where shares of listed Pakistani companies change hands. You do not buy from the exchange — you buy from another investor. The exchange is the venue plus the rulebook that makes the trade safe.

cards.h: The index is a weighted average
p: The KSE-100 tracks 100 of the larger listed companies, weighted so that bigger companies move it more. When the news says the market rose 1%, they almost always mean this index.
Because it is weighted, the KSE-100 can rise on a day when most shares fell — a few heavyweight banks or fertiliser names can carry it alone.
'The market' and 'my shares' are genuinely different things. The index being green tells you very little about what you own.

lessons.takeaway: The index is a weighted average of the big names, not a summary of every stock.

check.q: KSE-100 is up 0.8% but two-thirds of listed shares fell. Possible?
options: No — the index averages all shares equally
Yes — it is weighted, so a few large companies can lift it
Only if the exchange made an error
check.explain: This happens often, and it is why a green index says nothing reliable about your own holdings.

lessons.title: Your account, your broker, and what it costs
lessons.why: The practical step that stops most people — and where avoidable costs get locked in permanently.

p: To buy shares in Pakistan you need an account with a licensed broker — a TREC holder — and your shares are then held in your name at the Central Depository Company, the CDC.
The shares sit in a depository, not in your broker's pocket. That separation is the protection that matters most.
You can verify that a broker is genuinely licensed on the PSX and SECP websites before sending anyone money.
Do this. It takes two minutes and it is the single cheapest piece of due diligence available to you.

cards.h: Four questions to ask every broker
p: What is the commission per trade — as a percentage AND as a minimum rupee amount?
What else appears on a contract note: CDC charges, taxes, any annual fee?
Is there a minimum account balance?
Can I see a sample contract note before I open?

cards.h: The minimum commission is the one that hurts
p: If a broker charges a minimum of Rs 100 per trade and you buy Rs 5,000 of shares, you paid 2% to get in and will pay again to get out. The stock must rise roughly 4% before you break even.
This is why frequent small trades are so expensive relative to their size — and why this desk works on a daily timeframe rather than trading in and out.
Costs are certain. Returns are not. Know every charge before your first trade.

lessons.takeaway: Costs are certain and returns are not. Know every charge before your first trade.

check.q: Minimum commission is Rs 100 per side. You buy Rs 4,000 of shares and later sell. Roughly what must the price do to break even?
options: Rise about 1%
Rise about 5%
Nothing — commission comes out of the broker's profit
check.explain: Rs 100 in and Rs 100 out is Rs 200 on Rs 4,000 — about 5%. On small tickets, commission is the biggest thing between you and a profit.

lessons.title: The money rules that come first
lessons.why: Nearly every painful investing story starts with money that should never have been in the market.

p: Money you will need within about three years does not belong in shares. Prices can stay depressed for years, and being forced to sell at the wrong moment turns a temporary loss into a permanent one.
Keep an emergency fund in cash before you invest a single rupee. Its entire purpose is to stop the market from becoming your emergency fund.
Borrowed money adds a deadline and an interest bill to something that has neither guarantees nor a timetable.
This desk is long-only and never uses leverage, for exactly this reason.
Professionals are wrong a large fraction of the time. They survive because no single position can take them out.
Position size — how much of your money sits in any one name — protects you far more reliably than being clever about which name.
If someone messages you a stock with urgency attached, the urgency is the product being sold to you.

lessons.takeaway: Survive first. Returns are only available to people still in the game.

check.q: Which money belongs in shares?
options: Your emergency savings, so it grows faster
Borrowed money, if the tip is good
Money you can leave untouched for years and could afford to lose
check.explain: The market cannot be told when you need the money back. Only capital with no deadline and no obligation attached belongs here.

levels.title: The documents
levels.blurb: Every document a Pakistani listed company publishes, what each one is for, and how to actually read the three financial statements line by line.

lessons.title: The full map of company documents
lessons.why: Once you know what exists and what each is for, you never need anyone's WhatsApp forward again.

cards.h: Everyone is told at the same time
p: A listed company must tell the whole market the same thing at the same moment. That happens through announcements filed with the PSX.
This is the principle behind every document below: if it matters, it must be public, and it must be public to everyone at once.
Tap any document to see what it is, when it appears, and what to look for inside it.

If a claim cannot be traced to a filing, an audited statement or an official announcement, it is a rumour. The desk holds itself to the same rule — it quotes no price or date it cannot pull from its own data layer.

lessons.takeaway: Filings first. Everything else is commentary on filings.

check.q: A friend says a company is about to announce a big dividend. Responsible next step?
options: Buy before the announcement
Look for an actual filing or board-meeting notice and treat it as unverified until then
Forward it to more people to see if they agree
check.explain: Either it has been announced — in which case it is public and verifiable — or it has not, in which case your friend either does not know or should not know. Neither is a reason to act.

lessons.title: Inside the annual report
lessons.why: It is the fullest picture a company gives you all year, and most of it is readable without any accounting training.

cards.h: The one document worth an hour
p: The annual report bundles almost everything: audited financial statements, the auditor's opinion, the directors' report on what happened and why, the notes that explain the numbers, and the pattern of shareholding.
Quarterly accounts are lighter and unaudited, but far more current.
Tap a section to see what it tells you and the trap to watch for.
Experienced readers often start at the auditor's report, then the notes, then the statements, and read the glossy chairman's letter last.
The pictures are marketing. The notes are where the actual disclosures live — related-party transactions, contingencies, how revenue is recognised.
The notes are not an appendix. They are frequently the most informative part of the entire document.

lessons.takeaway: Auditor's opinion, then notes, then statements. The glossy pages last.

check.q: Where in an annual report would you find related-party transactions and contingencies?
options: The chairman's letter
The notes to the financial statements
The cover page
check.explain: The notes carry the disclosures that give the headline numbers their meaning — which is exactly why they are worth reading before the narrative sections.

lessons.title: The income statement, line by line
lessons.why: It answers the first question about any business: does it actually make money, and from what?

p: The income statement covers a stretch of time — a quarter or a year — and walks from what the company sold down to what was left for shareholders.
Every line below sits between those two ends. Learn the shape once and you can read any company's.
Tap any line to learn what it is and what to watch. Real reported figures are marked as such; the rest is the structure to look for in the filing itself.
Check whether profit grew because the business sold more, or because of a one-off: an asset sale, a tax reversal, a currency gain. The directors' report usually says.
One-offs do not repeat, and a company whose profit growth is entirely one-offs has not actually grown.

Finance cost — interest on borrowings — deserves special attention here. Policy rates in Pakistan have swung dramatically, and for a leveraged company that single line can decide between a reported profit and a reported loss.
Revenue is activity. Profit is what survives the costs. EPS is profit per slice.

lessons.takeaway: Revenue is activity, profit is what survives costs, EPS is profit per slice.

check.q: Revenue rose 20% but profit after tax fell. Which explanation is NOT plausible?
options: Costs rose faster than sales
Finance cost jumped after rates rose
Revenue growth always guarantees profit growth
check.explain: Everything between revenue and profit can move against you. Growing sales into shrinking margins is one of the most common ways a business disappoints.

lessons.title: The balance sheet, line by line
lessons.why: The income statement shows one year. The balance sheet shows whether the company survives a bad one.

p: A balance sheet is a snapshot: assets on one side, liabilities and equity on the other. It always balances, because equity is defined as whatever is left after subtracting what is owed from what is owned.
Tap any line to see what it means and what a healthy or worrying version looks like.

cards.h: Two ratios do most of the work
p: Current assets against current liabilities — the current ratio. Below 1 means short-term obligations exceed short-term resources. Not automatically fatal, but it demands an explanation.

Total debt against equity. High debt is not automatically bad — utilities and cement carry it by nature — but it converts a bad year into a dangerous one, because interest must be paid whether or not the company earns anything.
If receivables grow much faster than revenue, the company may be booking sales it has not been paid for.
In Pakistan, receivables from government-linked entities have been a real and recurring issue in certain sectors — the circular debt problem in energy is the clearest example.

Book value per share is equity divided by shares — the accounting value of your slice. A starting point, not an answer: assets are carried at accounting values, which may sit well above or below what they would actually fetch.

lessons.takeaway: Assets minus liabilities is your slice. Debt decides how much bad news the company can absorb.

check.q: Why does a heavily indebted company get riskier when profits fall?
options: Interest must be paid regardless of earnings
Lenders forgive debt in bad years
Debt disappears when profits fall
check.explain: Debt is a fixed claim; equity is the leftover. When earnings shrink the fixed claim is paid first and the leftover absorbs the entire shortfall — which is why leverage magnifies losses as well as gains.

lessons.title: The cash flow statement, line by line
lessons.why: Companies rarely fail because they were unprofitable. They fail because they ran out of cash.

cards.h: Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact
p: A sale becomes revenue when goods are delivered, not when the customer pays. So a company can report healthy profits while cash quietly drains away.
The cash flow statement is the antidote to that ambiguity.
Tap any section to see what it captures and what a warning sign looks like.
Operating cash flow against profit after tax, over several years.

If profit consistently exceeds operating cash flow, ask where the cash is going — usually receivables or inventory, sometimes a genuine problem. It is not proof of anything wrong, but it is the most reliable prompt to look harder.
A dividend is paid in cash. A company paying dividends it does not generate in cash is funding them from borrowings or reserves — which can continue for a while, but not indefinitely.

lessons.takeaway: Follow the cash. Profit can be shaped by judgement; cash either arrived or it did not.

check.q: Profit rises every year but operating cash flow is consistently far below it. Most sensible reaction?
options: Ignore it — profit is what matters
Investigate where cash is going, commonly receivables or inventory
Assume the auditors erred
check.explain: Persistent gaps between profit and cash deserve an explanation you can actually find in the notes.

lessons.title: The auditor's report and who owns the company
lessons.why: Two short sections that tell you whether to trust the numbers and whose interests actually run the business.

cards.h: The auditor's opinion is a verdict
p: An unqualified — 'clean' — opinion means the auditors believe the statements fairly present the company's position. This is the normal outcome.

A qualified opinion, an adverse opinion, or a disclaimer means something is wrong or could not be verified. Any of these is a serious signal that deserves reading in full before anything else in the report.

cards.h: Emphasis of matter, and going concern
p: An 'emphasis of matter' paragraph flags something the auditors want you to notice without qualifying their opinion.

A 'material uncertainty related to going concern' is the strongest warning in the document: the auditors are saying there is real doubt the company can continue operating. It is written in careful language and it is easy to miss if you are skimming.
This section lists who owns the company: sponsors and directors, associated companies, banks and funds, and the general public.
Free float — the portion genuinely available to trade — matters for liquidity. A very thin free float means the price can move violently on modest volume.
Look for dealings between the company and its own sponsors or associated companies. These can be entirely legitimate and routine.
They are also the mechanism through which value most often leaves a company in ways minority shareholders do not benefit from — which is why they are disclosed, and why they are worth reading.
Read the auditor's opinion before the numbers. It tells you whether the numbers are worth reading.

lessons.takeaway: A qualified opinion or a going-concern note outranks every other number in the report.

check.q: An annual report carries 'a material uncertainty related to going concern'. What does that mean?
options: A routine disclosure in every report
The auditors have real doubt the company can continue operating
The company changed auditors
check.explain: It is the strongest formal warning auditors give, written in restrained language. It is not routine, and it belongs at the very top of anything else you read about that company.

lessons.title: Announcements, AGMs and material information
lessons.why: This is the live feed — the documents that arrive between annual reports and move prices the same day.

p: 'Material information' is the legal term for anything a reasonable investor would want before trading. Companies must disclose it promptly.
The rule exists so that nobody can trade on something you have not been told.
A company must announce in advance that its board will meet to consider results or a dividend.
This is why results dates are knowable rather than surprises — and the desk will not open a new position into an unconfirmed results date for exactly this reason.
The annual general meeting is where shareholders formally approve the accounts and the final dividend, and where you may ask the board questions directly.
The notice of an AGM is itself a filing you can read. It carries the agenda, any special resolutions, and the book closure dates.
Between annual reports, the announcement feed IS the company's story. It is free, official, and almost nobody reads it.

lessons.takeaway: Announcements are the live feed. Board-meeting notices make results dates knowable in advance.

check.q: Why must a company announce a board meeting before it considers results?
options: So the market knows in advance and nobody trades on private knowledge
To attract media coverage
It is optional
check.explain: Advance notice is what keeps the information symmetric. It also means a results date is something you can plan around rather than be surprised by.

levels.title: Price, value and payouts
levels.blurb: What 'cheap' does and does not mean, how dividends actually reach your account, and why prices jump on results.

lessons.title: P/E, book value and the word 'cheap'
lessons.why: 'Cheap' is the most misused word in investing, and the most expensive one to misunderstand.

cards.h: A low price is not a low valuation
p: A Rs 12 share and a Rs 1,200 share tell you nothing about value until you know what each buys you in earnings, assets and cash.
Share price alone is one of the least informative numbers on the screen.

cards.h: P/E: what you pay per rupee of earnings
p: Price divided by earnings per share. At a P/E of 8 you are paying eight rupees for each rupee of last year's earnings.
Lower looks cheaper — but only if those earnings are durable.

P/E uses past earnings and a live price. If the market expects earnings to fall — a cyclical peak, a contract ending, a subsidy withdrawn — the price drops first and the P/E looks wonderfully low right before earnings collapse.
This catches beginners constantly. An unusually low P/E is a question, not an answer.
Price-to-book compares price to accounting equity. More useful for banks, where assets are largely financial; much less useful where the real assets are brands or people.
Dividend yield is annual dividend divided by price. A very high yield is a warning as often as an opportunity — yield rises when price falls, and the market may be pricing in a cut it expects.
No single ratio is a verdict. The desk values every stock four independent ways and takes the median, precisely because any one method can be badly wrong on any one company.

lessons.takeaway: Cheap means cheap relative to what you get. Share price alone tells you nothing.

check.q: A stock trades at a P/E of 4, far below its sector. First thing to consider?
options: It is definitely a bargain
The market may expect earnings to fall sharply, making the ratio misleading
P/E below 5 is impossible
check.explain: Sometimes the market is wrong. Often it knows something about next year's earnings that last year's number cannot show.

lessons.title: Dividends: the dates that decide if you get paid
lessons.why: The dates are strict, widely misunderstood, and getting them wrong means simply not being paid.

p: A share of profit paid out in cash. The board declares it, shareholders approve the final dividend at the AGM, and the company pays everyone on its register on a particular date.
Miss the middle one and you are simply not paid.

cards.h: The trap: '50%' does not mean 50% of the price
p: In Pakistan dividends are usually quoted as a percentage of face value, which is normally Rs 10. A '50% dividend' means Rs 5 per share.
It does not mean 50% of the market price. Confusing the two overstates the payout enormously, and it is one of the most common beginner errors.

cards.h: Why it is not free money
p: On the ex-date the price typically drops by roughly the dividend amount, because new buyers no longer receive that cash.
So buying just before the ex-date to 'collect' the dividend trades price for cash — and the dividend is taxed at withholding.
Own it before the ex-date, or the seller keeps the dividend. Sell on or after the ex-date and you still get paid.

lessons.takeaway: Own it before the ex-date, or you are not paid. A '50% dividend' means 50% of Rs 10.

check.q: A company declares a 40% dividend on Rs 10 face value. The share trades at Rs 200. You receive?
options: Rs 80
Rs 4
Rs 40
check.explain: 40% of the Rs 10 face value is Rs 4 per share — a 2% yield at Rs 200. Reading the percentage against the market price would have overstated it twentyfold.

lessons.title: Results season and why prices gap
lessons.why: Knowing when a company reports explains most of the sudden moves that otherwise look random.

p: Listed companies report quarterly through the year and publish audited annual results after year end. Boards announce meeting dates in advance, so results dates are knowable.

cards.h: Prices move against expectations, not against zero
p: A company can report record profit and fall, because the market already expected more.
This is the single most confusing thing for new investors — and entirely rational once you see that today's price already contains what people expect.
Results land outside trading hours, so the adjustment often arrives as a gap: the price opens well away from the previous close, with no chance to trade in between.
Anyone holding through it takes the full move in either direction. A stop-loss does not protect you across a gap.
For a long-term holder the day's move matters less than the trend: are margins holding, is debt rising, did cash follow profit? Those are answered in the accounts, not in the first hour's reaction.

lessons.takeaway: Prices move against expectations — and results gaps jump straight over any exit you planned.

check.q: A company posts record profit and the share falls 5%. Most likely reason?
options: The market expected even better, and the price already reflected that
Investors did not read the announcement
High profits always cause falls
check.explain: Today's price already embeds today's expectations. The move comes from the difference between what arrived and what was assumed.

levels.title: The desk's lenses
levels.blurb: How this desk tests an idea before trusting it — and how to read the astrology layer honestly.

lessons.title: What technical analysis claims
lessons.why: You will meet charts and indicators everywhere. Here is how to judge whether one is worth anything.

p: Technical analysis reads price and volume history for repeatable patterns, arguing that prices reflect collective behaviour and behaviour repeats.
Moving averages, momentum measures like RSI, and support and resistance levels are the common tools.
Patterns are extremely easy to see after the event. Point at any chart and you will find a shape that 'worked'.
That proves nothing, because you chose it already knowing the outcome.
Define the rule precisely. Apply it mechanically across long history. Subtract realistic costs. Then check it still works on data it was never tuned on.
Most rules fail this. The desk holds every strategy to exactly that bar and publishes the ones that failed.
A claim without a test is decoration. You are entitled to ask anyone showing you an indicator what happened when it was tested properly.

lessons.takeaway: Any pattern can be found in hindsight. Only out-of-sample testing separates rules from decoration.

check.q: Someone shows a chart where their indicator called three tops perfectly. What is missing?
options: Nothing — three correct calls is proof
Every time it fired and was wrong, plus costs, tested on data it was not chosen from
A prettier colour scheme
check.explain: Selected successes are not evidence. Without the full record the three wins may be the three cases they went looking for.

lessons.title: What 'proven' actually means
lessons.why: So you can read the Strategies page — and challenge anyone else's performance claims.

p: Win rate is the share of trades that made money. On its own it is nearly meaningless.
A rule that wins 90% of the time and loses catastrophically on the other 10% is a losing rule.
The average result per trade, wins and losses together, after costs. Positive expectancy means the rule made money on average when applied honestly.
Costs are not optional in this calculation — commission and slippage kill a great many rules that look good on paper.
Out-of-sample means the rule was checked on history it was never fitted to. Without it, a backtest measures how well someone tuned a rule to the past.
Lookahead bias is the classic way backtests lie: using information at a moment it was not yet available. It produces beautiful results that cannot be repeated in real life.
A rule with nine trades over nineteen years has not been tested; it has been glimpsed.
Be as suspicious of a small sample as of a missing one.
A strategy that cleared every bar is a rule that used to work, tested carefully. That is evidence, not a promise.

lessons.takeaway: Expectancy after costs, out-of-sample, on a real sample size. Win rate alone means nothing.

check.q: A strategy wins 80% of trades but has negative expectancy. Meaning?
options: It is profitable because it wins often
The rare losses outweigh all the frequent small wins
The calculation must be wrong
check.explain: Many small gains funding occasional severe losses — a very common and very dangerous shape, and exactly why win rate alone is never enough.

lessons.title: The astrology lens, taught honestly
lessons.why: The desk includes a Vedic astrology layer. You should understand both what the tradition says and what testing showed.

p: Vedic — sidereal — astrology is a centuries-old system with real internal structure. It measures planetary positions against the fixed stars rather than the seasons, which is why a sidereal chart differs from the Western one you may have seen.
The nine grahas are the bodies it tracks: the Sun and Moon, five planets, and the two lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu.

The zodiac divides further into 27 nakshatras, or lunar mansions. Your Moon's nakshatra anchors a Vedic reading, which is why the tradition often reads a chart from the Moon rather than the rising sign.
A dasha is a planetary period; gochara is the moving sky read against your birth chart.
The desk tested whether these signals predicted PSX returns — thousands of hypotheses, nineteen years of data, proper statistical correction. Nothing survived.
The same machinery, pointed at ordinary market factors, did find real effects: oil genuinely moves exploration and production stocks.
Holding both ideas at once — this is a rich tradition worth understanding, and it did not beat a fair test — is itself the skill this whole course builds.

lessons.takeaway: Real tradition, real mathematics, tested honestly, no demonstrated edge. Explore it as exploration.

check.q: How should the astrology layer inform what you buy?
options: As a timing signal, since the calculations are accurate
Not at all — it is exploration, and testing found no predictive edge
As a tiebreaker when other analysis is unclear
check.explain: Accurate astronomy is not predictive power. The mathematics being correct says nothing about whether the signal forecasts prices — and tested properly, it did not.

levels.title: Journey lessons
levels.blurb: Lessons that belong to the Investment Journey spine.

lessons.title: Why invest at all?
lessons.why: The honest case for owning shares — and the honest case against rushing in.

p: Money sitting in a current account buys a little less every year. Pakistan has lived through long stretches of high inflation, and in those years idle cash was not 'safe' — it was losing purchasing power with certainty.
Investing is not about getting rich quickly. It is about giving your savings a fighting chance of keeping and growing their real value.

cards.h: What a share offers that a deposit cannot
p: A deposit pays you a fixed return and hands the upside of the economy to someone else. A share makes you an owner: you hold a claim on a real business's profits, its dividends, and its growth.
Ownership is also riskier — profits are not promised, and prices swing. That trade is the whole subject of this journey.
It is not a substitute for an income, not a way to double money in months, and not a place for money you cannot afford to lock away.
Anyone promising otherwise is selling something.
You invest to put your savings to work in real businesses, accepting real risk, over years. If that sentence feels acceptable, keep going.

lessons.takeaway: Investing trades certainty for ownership. Do it with money that can stay, over years.

check.q: What is the strongest honest reason to invest in shares?
options: Guaranteed higher returns than a bank
Owning a claim on real businesses' profits and growth, accepting risk
Everyone else is doing it
check.explain: Nothing about shares is guaranteed. The case for them is ownership of productive businesses over time — with risk accepted, not denied.

lessons.title: Opening your PSX account, step by step
lessons.why: The practical wall between you and your first share. Lower than you think.

p: You open a brokerage account with a licensed broker (a TREC holder), and alongside it a CDC account where your shares are held in your own name.
Verify any broker's licence on the PSX and SECP websites before sending money — it takes two minutes.

The CDC offers a simplified account tier (Sahulat) designed for new, smaller investors: less documentation, faster opening, but with a cap on how much you can invest through it. The cap is revised from time to time — check the CDC's current figure rather than trusting any fixed number you read.
A full account has complete documentation and no such cap. Many people start with Sahulat and upgrade later.
Your CNIC, a selfie or in-person verification, your bank account details (IBAN), and for a full account, proof of income or a bank statement.
Expect a signature specimen, and expect the broker to ask about your profession and source of funds — that is a regulatory requirement, not nosiness.
Ask the four fee questions from the Foundations level: commission per trade (percentage AND minimum), all other charges on a contract note, any minimum balance, and a sample contract note.
Get the answers in writing. This is where avoidable costs get locked in.
Licensed broker, shares held at the CDC in your name, fees known in writing before the first trade. That is the whole checklist.

lessons.takeaway: Verify the licence, know every fee in writing, and your shares sit at the CDC in your own name.

check.q: Where are your shares actually held after you buy them?
options: In the broker's own account
At the CDC, in your name
At the PSX building
check.explain: The depository holds your shares in your name. That separation from the broker's own assets is your main structural protection.

lessons.title: Funding the account safely
lessons.why: Short, but this is where people get scammed. Three rules cover it.

cards.h: Bank to broker, in your own name
p: Fund the account by bank transfer from YOUR bank account to the broker's designated client account. The transaction leaves a paper trail with your name on both ends.
The broker's app or back office should show the deposit against your account within a working day or so — confirm it before trading.

cards.h: Never hand cash to an individual
p: No legitimate broker needs cash handed to an agent, a 'representative', or anyone's personal account. That is how money disappears.
If anyone asks you to deposit into a personal account name, stop and report it.
Start smaller than you think you should. Your first deposits are tuition — the goal is to learn the machinery with money whose loss would annoy you, not wound you.

lessons.takeaway: Your bank → the broker's client account → confirmed in the app. Never cash, never a personal account.

check.q: A 'broker's agent' asks you to deposit into his personal bank account to 'speed things up'. What is this?
options: A normal shortcut
A scam pattern — stop and report it
Fine if he shows a business card
check.explain: Client money goes to a designated client account with a paper trail. Anything else is the single most common way new investors lose money before buying a single share.

lessons.title: Choosing your first stock to STUDY
lessons.why: Not your first stock to buy — your first to understand. The order matters.

cards.h: Start with businesses you already touch
p: The bank you use, the cement in your house, the fertiliser behind your food, the fuel station you stop at, the milk brand in your fridge. Many are listed.
A business you encounter in real life is one whose fortunes you can reason about — which is the entire game.

Can I explain how this company makes money in one sentence? Is it actually profitable? Does it pay a dividend, and has it paid one reliably? Is its debt manageable? Does enough of it trade daily that I could get out?
You now know how to answer every one of those from the documents — that is what the last three levels were for.
Whatever moved 30% last month, whatever a WhatsApp group is excited about, and anything whose business you cannot explain.
Fast movers and rumour stocks are where new investors donate money to experienced ones.
Pick one company. Read its ticker page on this desk, then its latest annual report. When you can explain it to someone else, you have graduated from this step — without spending a rupee.

lessons.takeaway: Study one understandable, profitable, dividend-paying business before any money moves.

check.q: What qualifies a company as a good FIRST stock to study?
options: It rose the most last month
You can explain its business, it is profitable, and it trades with real liquidity
A group chat is confident about it
check.explain: The first company is for learning to read a business end to end. Understandability, real profits and the ability to exit are what make that learning possible.

lessons.title: How people actually lose money
lessons.why: Not from picking slightly-wrong stocks — from a handful of repeated behaviours. All avoidable.

cards.h: Buying the top of a run
p: The most common story: a stock has already doubled, everyone is talking about it, and that is precisely when new money arrives — buying from the people who bought earlier and are now selling.
Excitement is information about other people's positions, not about value.
Adding to a falling position is only sound if you can say specifically why the market is wrong — from the filings, not from hope.
'It was Rs 100 and now it's Rs 60, so it's cheap' is not a reason. Sometimes it is on its way to Rs 30 for reasons the annual report already disclosed.
Broad market falls drag good businesses down with bad ones. Selling everything in a downturn converts a temporary mark-down into a permanent loss.
This is why the money rules came first: money that cannot wait will always be sold at the worst time.
One stock going to zero should be survivable. If it isn't, the position was too large — regardless of how confident you were.
Spreading across a few sectors matters more than most stock-picking skill. Even this desk's own rules cap any position and forbid doubling up within a sector.
Nobody avoids being wrong. The survivors are the ones whose wrongness was affordable — sized small, spread out, and never on borrowed money or borrowed time.

lessons.takeaway: Losses come from behaviour — chasing, averaging blind, panic, concentration — more than from analysis.

check.q: A stock you own falls 40% and you cannot point to anything in its filings that explains it. What is the disciplined response?
options: Immediately buy more — it's cheaper
Immediately sell everything
Re-read the filings and recent announcements first; act on what you find, not on the price alone
check.explain: Price alone is neither a buy nor a sell signal. The move is to go back to the source documents and find out whether the business changed or just the mood.

lessons.title: Your watchlist: study before money
lessons.why: A watchlist is the bridge between reading about the market and being in it.

p: A watchlist is a small set of companies you have chosen to genuinely follow — reading their results, noticing their announcements, watching how their prices react to news.
Following five companies well beats skimming a hundred. Depth is the advantage available to small investors.
Star a stock anywhere on the desk and it follows you: your Today page surfaces your names first, and each carries its valuation, health and news at a glance.
Watch how your companies' quarterly results compare to what you expected. Being wrong in a notebook is free education.
Your action for this step: pick at least three companies you can explain, and star them. They become your training ground.

lessons.takeaway: Follow a few companies deeply. Your watchlist is where reading turns into judgement.

check.q: What makes a watchlist genuinely useful?
options: Having as many stocks as possible
Following a few understood companies deeply through results and news
Adding whatever moved today
check.explain: The point is building judgement on companies you understand — watching expectation meet reality, quarter after quarter. That only works at small scale.

lessons.title: Your first position — on paper
lessons.why: The final step is a real portfolio with virtual money. Every mechanic, none of the damage.

p: The practice portfolio gives you virtual PKR 500,000 at real market prices. Buying, position sizing, watching a red day, receiving a dividend — every mechanic of investing, experienced before any real money is exposed.
People learn faster from a falling position they actually hold — even a virtual one — than from any amount of reading.

cards.h: Practise the discipline, not just the trade
p: Size positions so no single one can ruin the portfolio. Spread across sectors. Write one sentence for why you bought — and what would make you sell.
If you cannot write the sentence, you are not buying a business; you are buying a price.
It cannot simulate fear. Real money hurts in a way virtual money never will, and everyone trades worse with feelings involved.
So treat your paper results as a ceiling, not a forecast — and go to real money smaller than your paper confidence suggests.
Your action: open the Practice portfolio and take your first position in a company you studied. Hold it through at least one set of results before you fund anything real.

lessons.takeaway: Paper first. Every mechanic is real except the fear — so treat paper results as your ceiling.

check.q: What is the one thing a practice portfolio cannot teach you?
options: How dividends are credited
How position sizing works
How you behave when real money is losing
check.explain: The mechanics transfer; the emotions do not. That is why the step after paper trading is going smaller with real money than your paper results suggest.

docmap.when: Once a year, after year end
docmap.what: The full picture: audited statements, auditor's opinion, directors' report, notes, pattern of shareholding.
docmap.look: Start with the auditor's opinion, then the notes.

docmap.what: Condensed, unaudited financials — much more current than the annual report.
docmap.look: Compare against the same quarter last year, not the previous quarter.

docmap.what: An independent verdict on whether the statements fairly present the position.
docmap.look: Anything other than a clean opinion. Going-concern language outranks every other number.

docmap.what: Management explaining the year: what moved, what they expect, why.
docmap.look: Whether profit came from operations or from one-offs.

docmap.what: The disclosures behind every headline number.
Who owns the company: sponsors, funds, banks, general public.
docmap.look: Free float. A thin float means violent moves on modest volume.

docmap.what: Advance notice that the board will consider results or a payout.
docmap.look: The date — this is how results become knowable in advance.

docmap.what: Anything price-sensitive a reasonable investor would want before trading.
docmap.look: Contracts, regulatory action, plant shutdowns, changes in control.

docmap.what: Agenda, special resolutions, book closure dates, proxy form.
docmap.look: Special resolutions — they change something structural.

docmap.what: Management presenting to analysts and investors, often with slides.
docmap.look: Guidance and capacity plans stated out loud.

docmap.what: The offer document for a company listing for the first time.
docmap.look: Use of proceeds, and the risk factors section.

docmap.what: An agency's view of the company's ability to service debt.
docmap.look: The direction of travel — an outlook change often precedes trouble.

income_statement.title: Income statement
income_statement.subtitle: for the year ended — covers a period of time

lines.what: The value of everything sold in the period.
lines.watch: The top line says nothing about profitability. A company can grow revenue for years while losing money.

lines.what: The direct cost of producing what was sold — raw materials, fuel, factory wages.
lines.watch: Rising faster than revenue means margin is being squeezed.

lines.what: Revenue minus cost of sales — what is left before overheads.
lines.watch: Gross margin only means something against the company's own history and its own sector.

lines.what: Getting the product to customers: freight, marketing, sales salaries.
lines.watch: A sharp rise with flat revenue suggests the company is buying growth.

lines.what: Head office, salaries, professional fees — running the company itself.
lines.watch: Should generally grow slower than revenue as a business scales.

lines.what: Profit from actually running the business, before financing and tax.
lines.watch: This is the cleanest measure of the operation itself.

lines.what: Interest on borrowings.
lines.watch: In Pakistan this line moves enormously with policy rates. For a leveraged company it alone can decide profit or loss.

lines.what: Income outside the main business — asset sales, investments, currency gains.
lines.watch: The classic home of one-offs. Profit that lives here does not repeat.

lines.what: What is left after financing, before the government's share.
lines.watch: Compare with operating profit to see how much financing is costing.

lines.what: Corporate tax for the period, including deferred tax.
lines.watch: An unusually low charge is often a one-off reversal, not a permanent improvement.

lines.what: The bottom line — what belongs to shareholders.
lines.watch: Check the cash flow statement to see whether this profit actually arrived as cash.

lines.what: Profit after tax divided by the number of shares — profit per slice.
lines.watch: The end of a long chain of judgements, not a fact of nature. Most valuation talk is built on it.

balance_sheet.title: Balance sheet
balance_sheet.subtitle: as at a single date — a snapshot, not a period

lines.what: Land, buildings, machinery — the productive base, after depreciation.
lines.watch: Compare with capital expenditure in the cash flow: is the company maintaining its base?

lines.what: Stakes in subsidiaries, associates or securities held for the long term.
lines.watch: In group structures this is where money moves between related companies.

lines.what: Goods made or bought but not yet sold.
lines.watch: Growing much faster than revenue suggests goods are not moving.

lines.what: Money owed by customers for goods already delivered.
lines.watch: The single most informative asset line. Growing faster than revenue means sales booked but not collected.

lines.what: Actual cash available.
lines.watch: Compare against short-term borrowings — cash alongside heavy short-term debt deserves a question.

lines.what: The face value of issued shares — usually Rs 10 each in Pakistan.
lines.watch: Divide by 10 to sanity-check the share count.

lines.what: Profits retained in the business rather than paid out.
lines.watch: The accumulated result of every year the company has traded.

lines.what: What shareholders own after every liability is settled. Divided by shares, this is book value per share.
lines.watch: Carried at accounting values, which may sit well above or below what assets would actually fetch.

lines.what: Borrowings due beyond one year.
lines.watch: Against equity, this is the leverage that turns a bad year into a dangerous one.

lines.what: Money the company owes suppliers.
lines.watch: Stretching payables is a quiet way to fund operations — and a sign of cash strain.

lines.what: Debt due within a year, including running finance.
lines.watch: Against current assets: can the company actually meet what falls due?

cash_flow.title: Cash flow statement
cash_flow.subtitle: for the year ended — where cash actually went

lines.what: The starting point, taken from the income statement.
lines.watch: Everything below adjusts this accounting figure back toward actual cash.

lines.what: Non-cash charges added back — depreciation reduced profit but no cash left.
lines.watch: Large adjustments are normal in capital-heavy sectors like cement and energy.

lines.what: Movements in receivables, inventory and payables.
lines.watch: This is where a profitable company's cash disappears. Consistently negative deserves explanation.

lines.what: Cash the actual business generated.
lines.watch: THE key comparison: against profit after tax, over several years. Profit consistently above this is a prompt to look harder.

lines.what: Cash spent on plant, property and equipment.
lines.watch: Against operating cash flow: a business that cannot fund its own maintenance from operations depends on lenders.

lines.what: New debt taken on, and debt paid back.
lines.watch: Persistent new borrowing alongside weak operating cash flow is the pattern to worry about.

lines.what: Cash actually paid out to shareholders.
lines.watch: Compare with operating cash flow. Dividends funded by borrowing can continue for a while, but not indefinitely.

lines.what: The three sections summed — how the cash balance moved over the year.
lines.watch: Read alongside which section produced it. Cash up because of borrowing is not the same as cash up from operations.
